## Defining Your own Functions

As outlined before the elementary functioncs can be used to perform basic calculations. 
```{julia}
my_variable_1 = 2.0
my_variable_2 = 1.0
my_result = my_variable_1 + my_variable_2
```
The same operation can be performed with a self defined function:
```{julia}
function my_sum(x,y)
    return x + y
end

my_result = my_sum(my_variable_1, my_variable_2)
```
To define a function you have to use the keyword `function` this will open an environment where you can define your functions. To end this environment you will have to put the keyword `end` at the end of your function. In addition to that you have to give the function a name (e.g. 'my_function').
```{julia}
#| output: false
function my_function()

end
```
In the next step you have to think about the arguments that the function should take (e.g. if you want to write a function that calculates the difference of to variables, you will need two input arguments). Inside the function you can define the actual operation with the input arguments. By using the keyword `retrun` before you end the function you can prescribe what the function should return:
```{julia}
#| output: false
function my_function(a,b)
    c = a - b
    return c
end
```
In your function you can also add further actions. For example you can add a statement that prints out the result of the calculation:
```{julia}
#| output: false
function my_function(a,b)
    c = a - b
    println("The difference between $a and $b is $c !")
    return c
end
```
After you have defined the function you can use it like any other function that we have used before (e.g. `typeof()` or `sizeof()`). 
To use the function you have to call it by writing the name of the function and put the needed input arguments inside de parentheses:
```{julia}
x = 12
y = 5
my_function(x,y)
```
Defining a function instead of coding the operation directly is especially useful if the action or calculation should be perfomed more than one time. 
## Try it on Your Own

Write a function that takes the radius of a circle as input argument and calculates the area and the circumference of the circle for 3 different values for the radius (e.g. 3 cm, 10 cm and 17 cm). 

Hind: The Area and the circumference of a circle can be expressed as: $A = πr^2$ and $U = 2πr$
